facts.statement: The genus Colymboides was first described by Milne-Edwards in 1867.
Three species are known: C. minutus described in 1867, C. anglicus in 1891, and C. metzleri in 2004.
facts.quote: subdivision: †C. minutus Milne-Edwards, 1867 †C. anglicus Lydekker, 1891 †C. metzleri Mayr, 2004

facts.statement: The genus Colymboides has the synonym Gavioides.
The genus contains three species of early loons that lived during the late Oligocene or early Miocene.
facts.quote: The genus Colymboides contains three species of early loon dating from the late Oligocene or early Miocene.

facts.statement: These birds are considered the earliest known unambiguous fossils of the order Gaviiformes.
facts.quote: They are considered to be the earliest known unambiguous gaviiform fossils.

facts.statement: The genus is usually placed in the subfamily Colymboidinae within the family Gaviidae, separate from the modern-type loons of the subfamily Gaviinae.
facts.quote: It is usually placed in the Gaviidae already, but usually in a subfamily Colymboidinae, with the modern-type loons making up the Gaviinae.

facts.statement: Researchers debate whether Colymboides belongs in the family Gaviidae or in a now-extinct family of primitive gaviiforms due to its distinct features.
facts.quote: But the Colymboides material is generally quite distinct from modern loons, and may actually belong in a now-extinct family of primitive gaviiforms.

facts.statement: Fossils were found in rocks located between the Atlantic Ocean and the former Turgai Sea.
facts.quote: between the Atlantic and the former Turgai Sea

facts.statement: The genus lived from the Rupelian to the Langhian stages, approximately 33.9 to 13.82 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Rupelian to Langhian (33.9 to 13.82 million years ago)

facts.statement: The parent group of the genus Colymboides is the family Gaviidae.

rejected.statement: The best-studied species, C. minutus, was described as being much smaller than modern loons and less adapted to diving.
rejected.quote: The best studied species, Colymboides minutus, was described by Robert Storer as being much smaller than modern loons and not as well adapted to diving.
